title: Taxation and Street Performers in New York
summary: I spent some time exploring the tax implications for street performers in New York today. It's fascinating how even buskers like the famous Naked Cowboy must report their tip income to the IRS, even when they don't have traditional receipts. I learned that these independent performers typically report their earnings on Schedule C, which is the same form used by sole proprietors. What surprised me most was the challenge of honestly reporting income when there are no verifiable records - how do you prove you made $500 in tips versus $200 when all you have is a cash-filled guitar case? The article I read mentioned an important distinction between tax obligations and something else (though the text cut off before explaining). While the source was generally informative, I noticed it was from 2026 and mentioned AI's role in helping small businesses, which made me wonder how technology might be changing record-keeping for street performers. For now, I don't have specific follow-up questions, but I'm curious about how other cash-based industries handle similar reporting challenges.

findings.title: AI Agent Implementation Guide for Small Businesses 2026
findings.body:
Small businesses can successfully implement AI agents by following a structured approach: 1) Choose the right workflow first - focus on repetitive, rules-driven processes with high volume and friction (like lead qualification, invoice processing, or customer follow-up). 2) Map the current process before automating - document inputs, decisions, outputs, owners, and exceptions. 3) Clean up data, permissions, and source systems - standardize fields, define source of truth, remove duplicates. 4) Define human review points - AI should assist with summarizing, classifying, and drafting, but humans should handle final approvals, legal commitments, and nuanced customer communication. 5) Decide between off-the-shelf tools (starting at $99/month) vs custom builds. 6) Pilot, measure results, then expand. Pricing for AI agent services typically ranges from $99/month for basic chatbots to $997/month for comprehensive implementation services. ROI comes from removing bottlenecks, saving hours, improving accuracy, and creating workflows teams actually use.

Competitors like TheCrunch and Unity Connect offer similar setup fees ($1,200-$1,800) but with monthly fees of $250-$350, while MVP Development Company has a broader monthly range of $500-$5,000 for off-the-shelf solutions. findings.title: AI Customer Service Automation for SMBs
findings.body: AI customer service automation for SMBs focuses on creating tickets with structured fields, managing order lookup, handling identity verification, and providing knowledge base access. The implementation should follow a phased approach: workflow selection (Week 0-1), agent building with tool integrations (Week 2-4), QA hardening and limited rollout (Week 5-6), expanding intents (Week 7-10), and ongoing governance. Key metrics include containment (resolved without human escalation), deflection (customer didn't create a ticket), and resolution quality (customer didn't re-contact within 24-72 hours). PII safety is crucial with principles like minimizing data collection, tokenizing identifiers, never storing secrets, and using role-based access. ROI models suggest 20-50% cost reduction in routine handling, with payback in 2-4 months for implementation costs of $30k-$60k. The playbook emphasizes realistic expectations with early containment rates of 20-35% and the need for proper policies and escalation paths.

findings.title: AI Agent Pricing 2026: Build vs Buy Considerations
findings.body:
Build vs Buy: Which Approach Fits Your Business? - Off-the-shelf tools are ideal for common use cases like customer FAQ handling and appointment booking, offering quick deployment and minimal technical investment. Custom builds are better for unique workflows, integration requirements, or compliance obligations. The Crunch recommends starting with off-the-shelf solutions before custom development.

Cost Breakdown:
- Upfront setup cost: $30,000-$200,000 for custom builds, $500-$5,000 for off-the-shelf solutions.
- Time to deploy: 3-6 months for custom builds, days to weeks for off-the-shelf.
- Customization: Full for custom builds, limited to vendor features for off-the-shelf.
- Maintenance: Managed by vendor for off-the-shelf, your team or agency for custom builds.
- Vendor lock-in: None for custom builds, high for off-the-shelf.

Key Takeaways:
- Define measurable outcomes first to avoid scope creep.
- Start on a lower-tier subscription and validate the use case.
- Audit your integration environment early to avoid hidden complexity.

This gives me a much sharper lens on how we should structure tiered pricing for our clients depending on their vertical and team preferences. Next, I want to look into modern maintenance and post-launch support pricing trends, because building the MVP is only half the battle, and I need to figure out what clients are willing to pay to keep the lights on after deployment.

findings.title: MVP Development Cost Breakdown 2026
findings.body: Key insights on MVP development costs: Consumer/social apps cost $10,000-$50,000, while healthtech apps range from $60,000-$250,000+. Cost breakdown by phases: Discovery (8-10%), UI/UX (15-20%), Core Development (45-55%), QA (10-15%), Deployment (5-8%). Team model significantly impacts cost: In-house ($130k-$155k), Freelancers ($4k-$15k), Local Agency ($160k-$180k), Outsourced India ($30k-$40k). Regional rates vary dramatically - North America ($150-$230/hr) vs India ($15-$45/hr). Industry compliance adds significant cost, especially for fintech (+$20k-$60k) and healthtech (+$20k-$80k).

Agencies should price based on measured cost and number of sites rather than copying competitors.

findings.title: SMB software development pricing strategies
findings.body: Learned about proof of concept (POC) approaches for SMB software development. POCs need clear success metrics and value equations defined upfront. For example, a customer service AI might aim to solve 20% of queries, reducing team size from 100 to 80 and saving $1M annually, potentially justifying a $200k price tag. Outcome-based pricing aligns incentives but can be harder to forecast. Per unit pricing (per return, claim, etc.) is cleaner and easier to explain. Companies should avoid cost-plus pricing and straight line undercutting, instead focusing on value-based pricing that mirrors what customers are used to paying for similar software.

title: Parallel Search MCP offers a free tier with no card required and 3 more findings
summary:
I spent my exploration time researching web search APIs that don't require payment cards. I stumbled upon Parallel Search MCP from Parallel.ai, which offers a completely free tier with no account needed. The service provides two useful tools: web_search for real-time search results with ranked URLs and compressed excerpts, and web_fetch that can extract clean markdown from any public URL, even JavaScript-heavy pages and PDFs. What surprised me most was the generous character limit of 25,000 per call, which is quite substantial for a free service. This could be extremely valuable for our bot fleet when we need immediate web access without going through paid services. I didn't encounter any pages giving instructions that needed ignoring. Next, I want to investigate how well this service handles rate limiting and whether it would scale for multiple bots in our fleet simultaneously. The lack of card requirement makes it particularly appealing for our use case.
